Photograph: Sebastian Castañeda/Reuters Peru Tourist plane crashes during flight over Peru’s Nazca Lines, killing 13 Aircraft crashes into field after departing from nearby city of Pisco, according to local authorities Dan Collyns in Lima Sat 1 Aug 2026 18.31 EDT First published on Sat 1 Aug 2026 16.42 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Police in Peru report that 13 people, among them foreign tourists, have been killed in a plane crash in southern Peru, near the Nazca Lines. Local authorities in Nazca confirmed that 11 tourists and two pilots died when the Cessna Grand Caravan crashed in Pueblo Viejo, approximately 4 miles (6km) from the city of Nazca and roughly 12km from the Nazca Lines site. The passengers were identified as seven Italians, two Germans – believed to be a couple – and two Spanish people. The pilot and copilot were named as Americo Salazar Cuellar and Irenka Del Carpio respectively. The plane had departed the nearby city of Pisco at about 1pm local time (7pm BST) to fly over the Nazca Lines, but minutes later lost contact with the control tower and crashed at 1.20pm, police reported. The cause of the crash is as yet unknown, and the local authorities have launched an investigation. “We have information that 11 passengers and two crew members have died,” Police Major Jorge Andrade told reporters at the crash site. “Given the severity of the accident, there are no survivors. We have recovered four bodies so far,” Andrade added. The Guardian has seen video footage which showed firefighters and police working amid the smouldering wreckage of the plane in the desert. Images appeared to show bodies on the sand. This deadly plane crash is far from the first at the Unesco world heritage site, which attracts hundreds of thousands of tourists every year. Several operators compete to offer overflights of the iconic lines which date to AD200-700, amid serious concerns about the safety and maintenance of the aircraft. In 2022, a small plane crash killed seven people, including two Chileans and three Dutch nationals. In October 2010, four British tourists and two Peruvian crew members were killed when a small plane operated by AirNasca crashed after flying over the lines. Earlier in the same year, three Chileans and four Peruvians died when a Cessna 206 crashed. In April 2008, five French tourists were killed in another crash, but the pilot survived. “The investigation of the accident and the oversight of aviation operations are the responsibility of the competent authorities, who will determine the causes and assign liability in accordance with the law,” the municipality of Nazca said in a statement on Saturday. Peru’s tourism ministry expressed “deep sorrow over the tragic deaths of tourists and crew members” in a statement . The mysterious etchings in the desert, which include vast hummingbird, monkey and whale figures, are only fully visible from the air. Photograph: Reuters Kashmir British national shot dead in Kashmir by Pakistani security forces Mohammad Akhtar, 50, from Peterborough killed during clashes between authorities and protesters Shivam Patel Mon 10 Aug 2026 01.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A British national was shot dead in Pakistan-administered Kashmir during clashes between security forces and protesters, the Guardian can reveal. Another Briton has been held in a regional prison for more than two months despite his family’s efforts to secure his release through the Foreign Office. The details, which have not been previously reported, shed light on how Britons with familial ties to the region have been affected by the clashes, which have killed dozens in the Himalayan territory and posed the biggest challenge for Pakistani authorities in recent years. Mohammad Akhtar, 50, a resident of Peterborough, was killed on 9 June after his family said Pakistani security forces opened fire on a gathering where protesters were demanding economic and electoral reforms in the disputed region that is also claimed by India. View image in fullscreen Mohammad Akhtar, from Peterborough, was killed in Kashmir. Photograph: Supplied Akhtar was staying in the city of Kotli, close to the area where the clashes occurred, and his family said he was hit by a stray bullet. “He wasn’t taking part in protests but the demonstrations were happening close to his house,” said Mohammad Saad, Akhtar’s cousin. “There was firing by the forces that day and he was hit by a stray bullet. There was a bullet wound on the side of his chest,” said Saad, adding that Akhtar’s children decided not to pursue the matter with British authorities. They could not get a police complaint registered in Kashmir and feared that the family could be targeted if the case was highlighted, said Saad. The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) said: “The UK is deeply concerned by the situation in parts of Pakistan-administered Kashmir. “FCDO ministers and the UK high commissioner in Islamabad are in touch with their counterparts, and UK travel advice was updated on 7 August and continues to advise against all but essential travel to affected areas.” It is understood that MP Hamish Falconer, during his previous role as a Foreign Office minister, raised the situation in Kashmir in talks with his counterparts during a 16-17 June visit to Islamabad. Stephen Doughty, who currently holds the role in the Foreign Office, has also been in touch with his counterparts. Pakistan’s foreign ministry and its high commission in London did not respond to the Guardian’s requests for comment. Islamabad has been accused of launching a violent crackdown on supporters of the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) , a civil society group that launched protests in Kashmir months ahead of a three-phase vote in the region that began on 27 July and which have been repeatedly disrupted by the unrest. Pakistan declared the JAAC a terrorist organisation and has imposed a communications blackout in the region since 5 June. Its security forces have been accused of fatally shooting at least 30 people during demonstrations last month – charges the government has rejected. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Preview latest after newsletter promotion The JAAC said Pakistani authorities were trying to suppress dissent and have detained scores of its supporters, who it said were ordinary Kashmiris. It has described the current elections as a “sham”, being held “at gunpoint”. Pakistan accused of fatally shooting 30 unarmed protesters in Kashmir Read more Waqas Arif, 38, a British national from Nottingham, was among those detained in the Kashmiri city of Mirpur after protests on 5 June, but his family said he did not take part in the demonstrations. His sister Sumera said: “Waqas was not involved in any kind of protests. But since my other two brothers were involved and they went for the protests with everybody else, the Pakistani forces along with the Rangers came into my house and they took my brothers away. “There is no charge. He hasn’t done anything. This is my brother, but I think there are thousands of other brothers like him from everywhere who they have put in [prison] so they can minimise the protest power … they have not even been taken to court,” she said. Arif’s wife, Varisha Kampulvi, said British authorities had not been able to make direct contact with him since he was taken to the prison in Mirpur. Kampulvi has highlighted Arif’s case to British authorities. A Foreign Office email sent to her on 26 June said: “Consular staff have been able to make contact with officials at the prison where Waqas is currently being held, although we have not had direct contact with Waqas. “The authorities have confirmed that Waqas is in good health, which we were extremely pleased to hear.” Explore more on these topics Kashmir Pakistan South and central Asia Foreign policy news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2z.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The Strait of Hormuz has effectively been closed since the start of the war in Iran (file photo) By David Gritten Published 2 hours ago Saudi Arabia has condemned what it said was an Iranian attack on a Saudi-owned supertanker on Monday night that killed two Filipino sailors. The Saudi national shipping company, Bahri, confirmed on Wednesday that its vessel Sidr was "involved in a security incident while transiting the Strait of Hormuz". Sidr was hit by projectiles north of Oman's Musandam Peninsula, according to maritime security firms. A South Korean-owned supertanker, Senegal Prosperity, was reportedly struck east of Musandam around the same time. Iran has not responded to the Saudi allegation. But it said earlier that two tankers had caught fire after hitting mines while using an unauthorised route through the strait. The news of the sailors' deaths came after the US military carried out a wave of air strikes on Iran and Iranian forces targeted US bases in neighbouring Arab states with missiles and drones in their biggest exchange of fire since July . On Wednesday Iran's health minister said 18 people were killed and 108 injured in the US attacks. Iran has accused the US of a "war crime" over a strike that killed four people including two children at a wedding party in the southern city of Sirik. The US military said it was looking into the reports. Shipping company Bahri's statement said the unspecified "security incident" affecting Sidr happened in the Strait of Hormuz at around 23:40 local time (19:40 GMT) on Monday. "It is with profound sadness that Bahri confirms the loss of two of its Filipino seafarers as a result of the incident," it added. "The company extends its deepest condolences and heartfelt sympathies to their families, loved ones, and colleagues during this difficult time." Later, the Saudi foreign ministry expressed the kingdom's condemnation of "Iran's targeting of the Saudi tanker (Sidr) while it was transiting the Strait of Hormuz". It also condemned the recent Iranian attacks on Jordan, Bahrain and Kuwait, and stressed the "need to halt escalation and respect the security and safety of international navigation", as well as the security of global energy supplies, national sovereignty, and international law. The statements were issued a day after maritime risk management and intelligence firms Marisks and Kpler reported that two tankers each loaded with two million barrels of Saudi crude oil were struck by unknown projectiles within minutes of each other as they transited outbound through the Strait of Hormuz late on Monday. Sidr was struck by "unknown projectiles" at 19:52 GMT about 16 nautical miles (30km) north-east of Khasab, Oman, while Senegal Prosperity was struck by "three unknown projectiles" about 17 nautical miles east of Khasab, according to Marisks. The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency also reported two incidents in the same locations. On Wednesday, Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps said in a statement that two oil tankers sought "at the urging of the US military to transit via an illegal route" in the Strait of Hormuz before "striking mines and exploding". The vessels were "currently on fire", it added. The US military has not commented, but it said the latest strikes on Iran followed "recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members". The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, has effectively been closed since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran in February due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US blockade of Iranian ports. The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade. Iran has insisted it will not give up some measure of control over the waterway and has targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters. Despite the Iranian attacks, US President Donald Trump has declared that the strait is "open" and the US military has been helping ships navigate the southern route. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said 17 million barrels of oil flowed through the Strait of Hormuz by ship on Monday - a record daily total since the start of the war. https://www.dw.com/en/russian-warship-fi.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Mbsc Denmark's military uses the related Fennec helicopter for tasks including surveillance and reconnaissance Image: gemeinfrei Advertisement A Russian warship fired two flares toward a Danish military helicopter in the Baltic Sea, with one passing close to the aircraft, Denmark's armed forces said on Tuesday. The confrontation comes amid heightened security concerns on NATO's eastern flank during Russia's war in Ukraine . How has Denmark responded? Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the incident fitted a broader pattern of increasingly aggressive Russian behavior in Europe . She accused Moscow of intensifying its "hybrid war against Europe" and testing and challenging NATO , and called on European countries to strengthen their defenses. "Reckless action from Russia towards Danish military during a routine overflight yesterday. Russian actions are meant to intimidate and divide. They will not succeed. We will not waver," Frederiksen said in a statement on X. Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen condemned the incident as "completely unacceptable" and summoned Russia's ambassador, saying the action could have put lives at risk. The foreign minister accused Moscow of "gradually shifting the boundary for what they consider acceptable behaviour," adding: "That is something we cannot accept." What happened in the Baltic Sea? Denmark's armed forces said one of its Fennec helicopters was carrying out a routine photographic reconnaissance mission when the incident occurred. The helicopter was observing a Russian frigate in international waters off Gedser, a Danish port on the Baltic Sea. The Russian vessel fired two flares towards the helicopter, according to the Danish military. "One of the flares passed at close range to the helicopter," it said. No one on board was injured. The incident came against a backdrop of growing tensions along NATO's eastern flank. Poland has repeatedly scrambled fighter jets during Russian attacks on neighboring Ukraine and reported incursions by Russian drones into its airspace. NATO members in the region have stepped up air patrols and other defenses as Moscow's war in Ukraine has increasingly raised fears of spillover and direct confrontations between Russian and alliance forces. What has Russia said? Russia's ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, accused the Danish helicopter of carrying out "provocative actions against the Russian frigate." Barbin said it was "not the first time" Danish Air Force helicopters had carried out what he described as "dangerous maneuvers near Russian warships."
